items.title: The UK was under 1 km of ice at the Last Glacial Maximum
items.claim: How extensively was Britain glaciated around 20,000 years ago?

options.text: Only the Scottish Highlands had ice
The British-Irish Ice Sheet covered most of the country north of the Thames-Severn line, with ice up to 1 km thick over the Highlands; southern England was a permafrost tundra
All of Britain was permanently glaciated until 1500

items.reveal:
The LGM (around 20,000 years ago) saw the British-Irish Ice Sheet extending to roughly the Thames-Severn line. Ice thickness over the Highlands exceeded 1 km. Glacial landforms record the maximum: corries (Snowdonia, Lake District), U-shaped valleys (Glencoe), drumlins (Eden Valley, Ribblesdale), erratics (the Norber erratics, Yorkshire).

The Younger Dryas (around 12,900-11,700 BP) was a final cold snap — the Loch Lomond Stadial — producing small Highland glaciers and ice caps. Britain was largely ice-free by around 10,000 years ago.

Britain rejoined Europe by land until the Storegga submarine landslide tsunami around 8,200 years ago finally severed Doggerland.
items.why: Most British landforms are products of the Quaternary Ice Ages, not earlier processes. The country's shape and soils are recent, contingent and shaped by ice.

items.title: 36 biodiversity hotspots hold around 50% of plant species

options.text: Regions with at least 1,500 endemic vascular plants and at least 70% original habitat loss — 36 defined globally by Conservation International, holding around 50% of plants and 43% of vertebrates
Only the Amazon and Congo basins

items.reveal:
Norman Myers identified the concept in 1988; Conservation International refined it. The 36 hotspots include Madagascar, the Atlantic Forest of Brazil, the Mediterranean Basin, the California Floristic Province, Sundaland, and more.

Total hotspot area is now about 2.4% of Earth's land surface — and yet holds the indicated share of species. Original extents were around 16% of land surface; the rest has been lost to human use.

IUCN Red List, BirdLife International's Important Bird Areas and the Alliance for Zero Extinction overlay related conservation priority maps.
items.why: Conservation cannot save every place. Hotspot prioritisation is one — contested — way of allocating effort to where it can save the most species. The trade-off with savanna, boreal and ocean priorities is real.

items.title: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean
items.claim: What does standard deviation tell you?

options.text: The highest value in the data
The typical (root mean square) deviation from the mean — about 68% of normally distributed data lies within one SD of the mean, 95% within two SD, 99.7% within three SD

items.reveal:
Standard deviation σ is calculated as the square root of the average squared deviation from the mean. For a normal distribution, the 68-95-99.7 rule applies — though many geographical datasets are not normal (skewed by extremes).

In fieldwork: comparing pebble sizes on two beaches, two questionnaire response distributions, or rainfall variability at two stations. A small SD means data cluster near the mean; a large SD means high variability.

Coefficient of variation (CV = SD/mean) allows comparison between datasets with different means — useful when comparing variability across scales.
items.why: Statistical literacy underpins geographical analysis. Reporting only a mean hides whether the data are tightly clustered or wildly variable — and the difference often matters more than the mean itself.
